Sanctions on Vietnamese Industrial Intermediate Producers Disrupt Supply Chains

A tightening series of international sanctions targeting Vietnam’s industrial intermediate products sector has begun to disrupt supply chains and halt operations at several key production sites, according to industry sources and trade associations.

The sanctions, imposed by a coalition of Western countries on Monday in response to ongoing geopolitical tensions in the South China Sea, have specifically targeted four major Vietnamese producers of chemical intermediates and metal components. Affected firms include Minh Tuan Materials, VietAlloy Processing, and two others, which together account for an estimated 37% of Vietnam’s intermediate product exports.

Customs authorities in the EU and North America have instructed ports and logistics companies to halt processing of imports of intermediate goods originating from these sanctioned firms. As a result, shipments of specialty alloys, industrial resins, and catalytic compounds remain stranded in containers at ports in Hai Phong and Ho Chi Minh City, with some vessels being denied entry or forced to reroute.

“In the last 48 hours, we have had over 200 containers held at the port, with no clear timeline for release,” said Doan Xuan Bao, operations manager at Minh Tuan Materials. “Our clients in Europe have already started seeking alternate sources, but we are still contractually obliged to deliver.”

The Vietnamese Intermediate Producers Association (VIPA) issued a statement late Tuesday warning of “immediate and severe” repercussions on production capacity and employment. “Many member companies are now unable to import critical inputs or export finished goods,” said VIPA chairwoman Tran Nhu Ha. “If the sanctions are not lifted soon, we expect layoffs and plant shutdowns within the next two weeks.”

Market analysts note that the sanctions come as Vietnamese producers were expanding capacity to meet rising global demand for intermediate goods used in electronics, automotive and advanced manufacturing. “The timing is particularly damaging,” said Le Huu Phat, a Hanoi-based supply chain analyst. “Just as firms were scaling up, they now face a sudden freeze in both upstream and downstream flows.”

As of Wednesday, workers at two VietAlloy Processing facilities in Bac Ninh and Dong Nai provinces reported being sent home on paid leave until further notice. The company’s management cited “force majeure” in communications to staff.

There is no indication yet when the sanctions might be reviewed or lifted. In the meantime, industry leaders are in urgent talks with Vietnamese authorities, seeking diplomatic solutions to restore trade flows and prevent broader fallout across the country’s industrial intermediate production hub.
